topics.title: Cerebrovascular System - Key Facts
topics.content:
Essential facts for cerebrovascular assessment and carotid scanning.

Key Facts:
• Carotid exam performed with patient supine, neck slightly extended, head turned away from side being scanned
• ICA = Internal Carotid Artery (low resistance vessel)
• ECA = External Carotid Artery (high resistance vessel)
• Vertebral arteries evaluated as part of cerebrovascular assessment
• 70-99% carotid stenosis is a CRITICAL FINDING requiring immediate attention
• Linear array transducer used for carotid exams
• Most common reason for underestimation of carotid stenosis = improper sample volume location
• Cursor should be placed at narrowest point of stenosis initially
• Move Doppler cursor through entire stenotic area to find highest velocity
• Bruit can be heard with stenosis, also with branching/tortuosity

topics.title: Cerebrovascular Normal Values
topics.content:
Normal hemodynamic values and waveform characteristics for cerebrovascular vessels.

Normal Values:
• ICA has increased acceleration time (AT) compared to high resistance vessels due to low resistance
• AT longer in ICA and cerebral vessels vs extremity arteries
• Brain vessels: Pulsatility Index (PI) normally <1.0
• ICA waveform: low resistance with continuous forward diastolic flow
• ECA waveform: high resistance with minimal/reversed diastolic flow

ICA Characteristics:
• Larger diameter than ECA
• Low resistance waveform
• Posterolateral position
• No extracranial branches

ECA Characteristics:
• Smaller diameter
• High resistance waveform
• Anteromedial position
• Multiple branches (superior thyroid, lingual, facial, etc.)

topics.title: Carotid Stenosis - Diagnostic Criteria
topics.content:
Comprehensive criteria for grading carotid stenosis and pathology findings.

Hemodynamic Significance:
• 50% diameter stenosis = 75% area stenosis = hemodynamically significant
• 70-99% stenosis = CRITICAL FINDING requiring immediate attention

Pathology Findings:
• Increased PSV and EDV at stenosis site
• Post-stenotic turbulence (eddy currents/vortices) distal to stenosis
• Spectral broadening at stenosis
• ICA/CCA velocity ratio helpful for grading stenosis

Carotid ICA Stenosis Criteria (NASCET):
• Normal: PSV <125 cm/s, no plaque
• <50%: PSV <125 cm/s, plaque present
• 50-69%: PSV 125-230 cm/s, ICA/CCA ratio <2.0
• 70-99%: PSV >230 cm/s, ICA/CCA ratio >4.0
• Occlusion: No flow

Signs of Stenosis:
• Elevated PSV at stenosis
• Turbulent flow
• Spectral broadening
• Post-stenotic turbulence
• Aliasing on color Doppler
• Dampened waveform distally

topics.title: Carotid Scanning Technique
topics.content:
Proper technique for comprehensive carotid duplex examination.

Patient Position:
• Patient supine with neck slightly extended
• Head turned away from side being scanned
• Pillow under shoulders if needed
• Technologist usually sits at head of bed

Transducer:
• Linear array transducer
• Typically 5-12 MHz
• Lower frequency for deeper vessels

Scanning Protocol:
• Scan entire length of CCA, ICA, ECA, and vertebral arteries
• Multiple angles through stenosis to find peak velocity
• Doppler angle ≤60 degrees (ideally 45-60°)
• Sample volume centered in vessel at narrowest point
• Move cursor through entire stenotic area to find highest velocity

B-Mode Imaging:
• Longitudinal and transverse views
• CCA (proximal, mid, distal)
• Carotid bulb
• ICA (proximal, mid, distal)
• ECA (proximal)
• Vertebral artery origin and V2 segment

Color Doppler:
• Identify areas of stenosis (aliasing, turbulence)
• Evaluate plaque morphology
• Confirm vessel patency

Spectral Doppler Measurements:
• ICA PSV and EDV
• CCA PSV and EDV
• ICA/CCA ratio
• Plaque location and characteristics

topics.title: Arterial Waveform Types
topics.content:
Understanding different arterial waveform patterns and their clinical significance.

TRIPHASIC WAVEFORM (Normal):
• Systole: rapid antegrade flow
• Early diastole: retrograde flow
• Late diastole: small amount of forward flow
• Seen in high resistance vascular beds (extremities/muscles)
• Normal in healthy extremity arteries
• Indicates normal resistance, no proximal stenosis

BIPHASIC WAVEFORM:
• Systole: antegrade flow
• Diastole: some retrograde flow (less than triphasic)
• Loss of late diastolic forward component
• Can be normal in older patients
• ABNORMAL if seen in organ vessels
• May indicate mild disease or vasoconstriction

MONOPHASIC WAVEFORM:
• Antegrade flow continues through entire cardiac cycle
• No retrograde component
• Rounded, dampened appearance
• Normal in vessels feeding organs (low resistance)
• ABNORMAL if seen in extremity arteries (indicates significant proximal disease or vasodilation)

TARDUS PARVUS:
• Delayed systolic upstroke (tardus = slow)
• Decreased amplitude (parvus = small)
• Rounded peak
• Prolonged acceleration time
• Indicates severe proximal stenosis or occlusion

topics.title: Velocity Measurements & Indices
topics.content:
Key velocity measurements and hemodynamic indices used in vascular assessment.

PEAK SYSTOLIC VELOCITY (PSV):
• Increases at stenosis site due to body maintaining blood volume
• Measured at narrowest point of stenosis
• Velocity increases as vessel diameter decreases
• Continuity principle: flow volume remains constant

END DIASTOLIC VELOCITY (EDV):
• Increases at stenosis site
• If EDV = 0 cm/s, then RI = 1.0
• Reflects downstream resistance
• Low in high resistance beds, higher in low resistance

RESISTIVE INDEX (RI):
• Formula: RI = (PSV - EDV) / PSV
• Extremity arteries: 0.6-0.8
• Organ vessels: <0.6
• If EDV = 0, then RI = 1.0
• Evaluates tissue resistance
• Not dependent on angle

PULSATILITY INDEX (PI):
• Formula: PI = (PSV - EDV) / mean velocity
• Organs: usually <1.5
• Brain: <1.0
• CFA: >5.0
• Popliteal artery: >8.0
• Values increase with distance from aorta
• Not dependent on angle

topics.title: High vs Low Resistance Patterns
topics.content:
Understanding vascular resistance patterns and their physiologic basis.

HIGH RESISTANCE PATTERN:
• Supplies extremities/muscles at rest
• Triphasic waveforms with retrograde diastolic flow
• Minimal or no forward diastolic flow
• Examples: ECA, resting limb arteries
• Vasoconstriction increases pulsatility
• Clenching fist increases distal resistance and pulsatility in proximal arteries

LOW RESISTANCE PATTERN:
• Supplies organs needing constant blood flow
• Monophasic waveforms with continuous forward flow
• Significant diastolic flow component
• No flow reversal
• Examples: ICA, renal, mesenteric, hepatic arteries
• Vasodilation decreases pulsatility

PHYSIOLOGIC EFFECTS:
• Vasoconstriction: changes monophasic to biphasic/triphasic
• Vasodilation: changes triphasic to monophasic
• Cold patient: vasoconstriction increases arterial resistance
• Warm patient: vasodilation decreases arterial resistance
• Exercise: vasodilation in muscles, increased flow
• Fist clenching: increases resistance, more pulsatile proximally
• Upon fist release: resistance drops, pulsatility reduced, flow increases

CARDIAC FACTORS:
• Decreased cardiac function = decreased output = reduced peak arterial velocities
• Increased cardiac function = increased output = increased peak arterial velocities
• Cardiac output affects all arterial velocities systemically
• Velocity ratios help normalize for cardiac output variations

topics.title: Basic Flow Principles
topics.content:
Fundamental principles of blood flow dynamics.

LAMINAR FLOW:
• Normal flow pattern
• Concentric layers of flow
• Parabolic velocity profile - fastest in center, slower near walls
• Narrow spectral bandwidth
• Clear spectral window
• Normal in straight vessels

PLUG FLOW:
• All layers same speed
• Flat velocity profile
• Occurs in systole in large vessels
• At branch origins
• Proximal to stenosis

TURBULENT FLOW:
• Chaotic, disorganized flow
• Disrupted, random velocities and directions
• Occurs with stenosis, post-stenotic, or high velocities
• Creates spectral broadening on Doppler
• Wide spectral bandwidth, filled spectral window
• Post-stenotic turbulence with eddy currents and vortices

REYNOLDS NUMBER:
• Predicts laminar vs turbulent flow
• >2000 = turbulent flow likely
• Factors: velocity, diameter, density, viscosity

POISEUILLE'S LAW:
• Flow = (ΔP × π × r⁴) / (8 × η × L)
• Flow is proportional to radius to the 4th power
• Small changes in diameter dramatically affect flow
• Small changes in vessel radius = most significant changes in flow
• Resistance proportional to 1/radius⁴
• Increased vessel radius = dramatically decreased resistance
